a1.say: Let's solve Two Baskets of Fruit, using the Sliding Window approach.

a1.cap: Trees stand in a row and fruits[i] is the kind of fruit on tree i. You have two baskets, each holding one kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.
a1.say: Trees stand in a row and fruits at i is the kind of fruit on tree i. You have two baskets, each holding one kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.

lines: Trees stand in a row and fruits[i] is the kind of fruit on tree i. You have two baskets, each holding one kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.

a1.cap: For example, with fruits = [1,2,1], the answer is 3.
a1.say: For example, with fruits equals 1, 2, 1, the answer is 3.

a1.cap: We want the longest window with at most two different kinds. Count kinds in the window with a map.
When a third kind appears, move L forward and decrease counts until one kind disappears completely.
Let's walk through it with fruits = [1,2,3,2,2].
a1.say: Let's walk through it with fruits equals 1, 2, 3, 2, 2.

a1.cap: Pick fruit 1. Kinds in the baskets: 1.
Pick fruit 2. Kinds in the baskets: 2.
Pick fruit 3. Kinds in the baskets: 3.
Three kinds is too many, so L moves to 1.
Pick fruit 2. Kinds in the baskets: 2.
Pick fruit 2. Kinds in the baskets: 2.
Time complexity is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of n and extra space is O of one.

a1.cap: That's the Sliding Window approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
